params.question: Every child presenting with acute suppurative otitis media should undergo HRCT of the temporal bone to exclude complications.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: ASOM is a clinical diagnosis. Routine imaging exposes children to unnecessary radiation. HRCT and MRI are reserved for red flags — post-auricular swelling, facial nerve palsy, vertigo, or altered consciousness — which suggest the infection has spread beyond the middle-ear cleft.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. ASOM is a clinical diagnosis — earache, fever, and a bulging eardrum warrant antibiotics, not a CT scan. Imaging only adds unjustified radiation unless red flags such as post-auricular swelling, facial palsy, vertigo, or altered consciousness suggest the infection has escaped the middle-ear cleft.

interactions.label: A patient with CSOM has undergone mastoid surgery for cholesteatoma. On follow-u

params.question: A patient with CSOM has undergone mastoid surgery for cholesteatoma. On follow-up, the surgeon suspects recurrence. Which imaging modality best distinguishes recurrent cholesteatoma from post-operative granulation tissue?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HRCT maps bone with exquisite clarity but cannot distinguish one soft tissue from another — cholesteatoma, granulation, and pus all appear identical on the bone window.
Correct. Cholesteatoma's packed keratin restricts water diffusion, appearing bright on DWI. Granulation tissue does not restrict diffusion, allowing reliable distinction without re-opening the ear.
Plain mastoid radiographs are now obsolete. They cannot resolve the scutum, ossicles, or critical canals needed for modern surgical decisions.

answers.text: Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted MRI of the internal auditory meatus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the IAM is used to screen for vestibular schwannoma in sensorineural hearing loss, not to evaluate post-mastoidectomy cholesteatoma recurrence.

overallFeedback.feedback: HRCT shows bone detail but all soft tissue looks the same. Non-echo-planar DWI-MRI resolves this: cholesteatoma restricts water diffusion and appears bright; granulation tissue does not.
Non-echo-planar DWI-MRI is the key modality — cholesteatoma restricts diffusion (bright on DWI), granulation tissue does not.

interactions.label: HRCT of a patient with cholesteatoma reveals erosion of the tegmen tympani, and

params.question: HRCT of a patient with cholesteatoma reveals erosion of the tegmen tympani, and contrast MRI shows a filling defect in the sigmoid sinus. What is the most important immediate change in management?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Canal-wall-up mastoidectomy is appropriate for limited cholesteatoma with an intact posterior canal wall — not when tegmen erosion and sigmoid sinus thrombosis indicate intracranial spread.

answers.text: Arrange serial MRI surveillance every six months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Serial MRI surveillance is the approach for small vestibular schwannomas confined to the internal auditory canal. Active intracranial complication from CSOM requires urgent intervention, not watchful waiting.

answers.text: Convert to an emergency procedure with neurosurgical backup and consider anticoagulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Tegmen erosion signals intracranial spread and a sigmoid sinus filling defect confirms venous thrombosis. The entire plan compresses: the case becomes a surgical emergency, neurosurgical backup is called, and anticoagulation joins the management.

answers.text: Obtain a non-echo-planar DWI-MRI to confirm the cholesteatoma before any intervention

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While DWI-MRI can confirm cholesteatoma, the critical finding here is intracranial complication — tegmen erosion and sinus thrombosis demand immediate action, not further diagnostic workup.

overallFeedback.feedback: When HRCT shows tegmen erosion and MRI confirms sigmoid sinus thrombosis, the infection has reached intracranial structures. This converts an elective cholesteatoma operation to a surgical emergency requiring neurosurgical backup and consideration of anticoagulation.
Tegmen erosion plus sigmoid sinus thrombosis converts an elective case to a surgical emergency with neurosurgical backup and anticoagulation.

interactions.label: A 3-year-old child with congenital profound sensorineural hearing loss is evalua

params.question: A 3-year-old child with congenital profound sensorineural hearing loss is evaluated for cochlear implantation. Heavily T2-weighted MRI shows an absent nerve in the anteroinferior quadrant of the internal auditory meatus. What does this finding mean for implant candidacy?

answers.text: The finding is a normal anatomical variant and cochlear implantation can proceed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An absent cochlear nerve is not a normal variant — it is aplasia, the single most important contraindication to cochlear implantation.

answers.text: Cochlear implantation can proceed because the implant stimulates the cochlea directly, bypassing the nerve

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A cochlear implant converts sound into electrical signals delivered to the cochlear nerve. Without the nerve, there is no neural pathway to carry those signals to the brainstem — the implant cannot function.

answers.text: Cochlear implantation is ruled out because the implant requires an intact cochlear nerve to transmit signals to the brainstem

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The cochlear nerve carries electrical signals from the implant to the brainstem. Its absence means the implant has no neural pathway to stimulate, making cochlear implantation futile.

answers.text: The child needs HRCT of the temporal bone before any decision can be made about implantation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While HRCT may be added to assess cochlear lumen patency, the T2W MRI finding of cochlear nerve aplasia is itself definitive — it rules out cochlear implantation regardless of what HRCT shows.

overallFeedback.feedback: An absent cochlear nerve on heavily T2-weighted MRI means the implant has no nerve to stimulate. This single finding rules out cochlear implantation entirely.
Cochlear nerve aplasia on T2W MRI is the single finding that closes the door on cochlear implantation — the implant needs an intact nerve to function.

interactions.label: A 55-year-old man presents with six months of progressive right-sided hearing lo

params.question: A 55-year-old man presents with six months of progressive right-sided hearing loss and poor speech discrimination scores. His left ear is normal. Which is the most appropriate first imaging investigation?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HRCT excels at imaging bone and is used for CSOM evaluation or congenital bony causes of hearing loss. For progressive unilateral SNHL, the primary concern is a retrocochlear soft-tissue mass — a question CT cannot answer well.
Plain mastoid radiographs are obsolete. They cannot visualise the internal auditory canal or cerebellopontine angle where a vestibular schwannoma would arise.

answers.text: Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal auditory canals and cerebellopontine angles

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Unilateral progressive SNHL with poor speech discrimination raises the clinical fear of vestibular schwannoma. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the modality of choice — a schwannoma enhances avidly and is centred on the IAM.

answers.text: Non-echo-planar diffusion-weighted MRI of the temporal bone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Non-echo-planar DWI-MRI is the sequence used to distinguish cholesteatoma from granulation tissue in CSOM. For suspected retrocochlear pathology, gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted MRI is the appropriate choice.

overallFeedback.feedback: Progressive unilateral SNHL with poor speech discrimination demands gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal auditory canals and cerebellopontine angles. The clinical fear is vestibular schwannoma — a soft-tissue mass that MRI, not CT, can reveal.
Asymmetric or unilateral SNHL with poor discrimination is a red flag for vestibular schwannoma — gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the IAM and CPA is the investigation of choice.
